body: The Middle East crisis and the spiking oil and gas prices have shifted the Asian nations' priorities to energy security and generating electricity with homegrown resources. Renewable energy capacity is soaring, not only in the top emerging markets China and India, but also across Southeast Asia, as the Strait of Hormuz crisis hiked LNG prices and dented gas demand. Another clean energy source, nuclear capacity, is also gaining momentum globally. Countries worldwide started thinking about adding or building nuclear reactors for the first time…

title: ICYMI: Fed's Jefferson says inflation is the key signal for rates, with PCE still at 3.6%
body: Jefferson's comments support pricing for a December hike without adding to the half-point tail, which suits the steady, gradual camp. By naming energy as the main channel for broader inflation, he makes Fed expectations sensitive to oil. Any renewed jump in crude tied to the Iran war and Hormuz shipping risk would feed quickly into rate pricing and the US dollar. His upbeat view on growth and jobs also removes an easy reason to pause. That keeps front-end Treasury yields supported, and continues to put gold under pressure from the Fed's tightening path. --- With unemployment steady and growth near potential, Jefferson has made it plain that inflation, and energy-driven inflation in particular, now sets the Fed's course. Summary: Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the trajectory of inflation is the most important signal for setting monetary policy. He said further moves should depend on data trends, the outlook and the balance of risks. Headline PCE inflation was 3.6% in September and core PCE was 3.1%. October data so far shows pressures staying well above target. He is concerned that higher energy prices could cause a broader, persistent rise in inflation, already visible in airfares and transport. Unemployment was 4.1% in October, which he sees as consistent with maximum employment. Q3 GDP grew at an annualised 3.4%. He voted with the majority to hold rates in October.

title: Weekend: Bessent urges Nvidia to hire an outsider CEO, pouring cold water on a Huang comeback
body: Bessent's comments make Nvidia's leadership question a political one. With a cabinet official openly favouring an outside hire, a Huang return becomes harder for the board to justify, and the recent rally in comeback hopes looks fragile. The 10-day deadline puts a near-term overhang on the stock beyond Tuesday's results, since any finding that sales to China-linked shell companies were knowingly pursued could bring penalties or tighter export curbs. His opposition to new legislation offers chip stocks some relief, but bipartisan momentum in Congress means export-control risk is still high for the wider semiconductor sector. --- Just as Huang's allies were building a comeback campaign, Washington weighed in: the Treasury Secretary wants an outsider in charge and answers on Nvidia's China sales within 10 days. Summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia needs a dramatic leadership shakeup and should look outside the company for its next CEO. His remarks came as Jensen Huang was reported to be discussing a return, backed by Silicon Valley allies. Bessent wants to know whether Nvidia ignored warning signs that shell companies, many in Singapore, were funnelling its AI chips to China. He said the board and its outside counsel should provide answers within the next 10 days. He opposed new legislation to lock in chip export controls, saying existing rules need enforcing. Nvidia shares fell about 12.5% last week. Interim CEO Colette Kress presents results on Tuesday.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6771 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: ECB bond market intervention warning from Governor Knot. Can't replace sound fiscal policy,
body: Knot's line on fiscal discipline matters most for euro zone sovereign spreads, especially French bonds against German Bunds. Markets will read it as a reminder that ECB support would be conditional rather than open-ended. A president with that view could make investors less willing to bet on a full central bank backstop if French finances get worse, which risks wider spreads during periods of stress. On rates, his cautious, data-driven stance on energy-driven inflation is softer than the hike signals coming from more hawkish policymakers, so a Knot presidency would lean toward patience rather than front-loaded tightening. The leadership race is now a live factor for the euro and for periphery bonds. --- Knot is pitching himself as an ECB chief who will steady bond markets in a crisis but won't bail out lax budgets, a message aimed at Paris as much as at the markets. Summary: Former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot said ECB bond-market interventions cannot replace responsible fiscal policy. He said the ECB can act to stabilise disorderly sovereign bond trading, but that is no substitute for sustainable public finances. Concerns about France's public finances have revived fears of another euro zone debt crisis. Knot is competing with Pablo Hernandez de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde, who leaves on February 7. He backed a cautious, data-driven approach on rates. The Iran war has lifted energy prices, but there is limited evidence of second-round effects.

title: Trump out of public view since Wednesday, fuelling speculation on his wherabouts
body: For markets, this is a non-event as long as the official record keeps showing normal activity. Traders have learned to discount social media speculation about the president's health, and nothing so far has moved oil, Treasuries or the US dollar on this story. The risk lies in his travel plans. A smooth departure for China would close the story, but an unexplained delay or cancellation would quickly become a factor for markets. With the Iran war still shaping energy prices, any real uncertainty at the top would tend to lift oil's risk premium and support safe-haven demand for the dollar. --- Trump's few days out of view have set off the usual online rumours, but the documented record shows a president working behind closed doors, and an expected trip to China this week should put him back in front of the cameras. Summary: Trump has not made a public appearance since Wednesday. His last sighting was a privately recorded White House interview on Thursday. The White House called a travel and photo lid on Saturday, a routine notice that the president won't be seen. His Sunday schedule showed a full day of calls and meetings, and he posted that he was working at the White House. Calendar entries also show a visit to his golf club. He has not publicly addressed Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop, which cabinet officials have handled. Speculation online about his health has no supporting evidence in the public record.

title: Weekend - Blackstone's QTS cuts AI data center debt sale 60% as investors push back on pricing
body: For credit markets, the QTS cutback is an early sign that the price of financing AI infrastructure is starting to matter. Investors are putting limits on how much they will hold of repeat issuers and on concentrated exposure to the sector. If that spreads, data center and AI-linked borrowers could face wider spreads or smaller deals, pushing more issuance into private credit and project finance at higher cost. For equities, any rise in funding costs feeds into the capex economics behind the AI trade. That is a sensitive point for sentiment this week, with Nvidia due to report on Tuesday. The deal is small, so it is not a credit event, but it is a signal worth tracking in future AI debt deals. --- Big week for AI ahead: Anthropic IPO six times oversubscribed: what retail investors can realistically expect --- The AI build-out has had seemingly unlimited access to capital, but QTS's shrunken deal shows that even a Blackstone-backed borrower now has to choose between paying up and settling for less. Summary: QTS, a Blackstone-backed data center operator, cut a planned private debt sale by about 60%. It is raising about $300 million, down from an initial target of roughly $800 million. Some investors objected to pricing, while others were limited by QTS's repeated use of the private placement market. QTS has raised billions through at least two private placements in 18 months, including a $1.65 billion high-grade sale last year.

title: ICYMI - Trump extends Jones Act waiver 90 days, foreign tankers moving oil in US
body: For oil, the extension is a small but useful relief valve rather than a supply story. It does not add barrels to the market, but it moves them more efficiently between US regions. That should help limit regional price spikes in gasoline and diesel, particularly on the East and West coasts, which depend on waterborne deliveries. The fact that most of the extra volume has been refined products suggests the main effect is on product cracks and regional spreads rather than on benchmark crude. Since the administration is still relying on emergency measures like this, traders should take it as a sign that Washington does not expect fuel prices tied to the Iran war to ease soon. --- Earlier: Iran says supertanker with 2 million barrels sank after Hormuz mine strike, unconfirmed --- Washington has again set aside a century-old shipping protection in the name of cheaper fuel, a sign that the Iran war's pressure on gasoline and diesel prices is still running ahead of political sensitivities over shipbuilding. Summary: President Trump extended a waiver of the Jones Act for 90 days, letting foreign-flagged ships carry oil and commodities between US ports. It is already the longest waiver in the history of the more than 100-year-old law. A blanket waiver was issued in March, a month after the US launched the war on Iran. It moved to case-by-case approval in August, which continues.

title: Iran says supertanker with 2 million barrels sank after Hormuz mine strike, unconfirmed
body: Oil is the main channel for this news. A claimed sinking of a fully laden supertanker in the world's most important crude chokepoint is likely to add to the risk premium in Brent and WTI when markets reopen (futures at 6pm Sunday, US Eastern time), even without independent confirmation. The bigger risk is about behaviour rather than barrels. If shipowners conclude that the US-cleared lanes and covert transits are not safe, Hormuz flows could shrink further, and freight rates and war-risk insurance costs could climb. If the claims are not confirmed, or are shown to be overstated, part of any initial jump could fade quickly, given how many similar Iranian announcements markets have already absorbed. --- Friday news ICYMI: Iran's Guards claim strike on US radar in Bahrain, warn firms over Hormuz oil trade --- Iran says its mines have sunk a laden supertanker in the Gulf, a claim no one else has yet confirmed, but its warning to ships using unapproved Hormuz routes is aimed squarely at oil markets and shipowners. Summary: Iran's IRGC Navy said two tankers with transponders off hit mines on an unauthorised route in the southern Strait of Hormuz. It said a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude sank in the southern Gulf, and the second tanker was still on fire. Iran's regular Army Navy described a single tanker hitting a mine and catching fire in a prohibited zone east of the strait.

body: Japan's GDP Price Index rose 2.4% year-over-year in the third quarter of 2026, easing slightly from the 2.6% increase recorded in the second quarter of 2026. The latest reading, updated on 15 November 2026, points to a modest cooling in overall price pressures across the Japanese economy. On a year-over-year basis, the indicator compares price levels in the third quarter of 2026 with the same period a year earlier, while the previous figure reflected the change in the second quarter versus its year-ago level. The step down from 2.6% to 2.4% suggests that, although inflationary pressures remain present, the pace of price growth is showing early signs of moderation. Market participants and policymakers are likely to view the softer reading as an indication that earlier price surges may be stabilizing, though the GDP Price Index remains above levels typically associated with very low inflation. title: Japan's External Demand Swings Negative in Q3, Undercutting GDP Momentum
body: Japan's external demand sharply reversed in the third quarter of 2026, with the indicator falling to -0.6% quarter-over-quarter from a revised 0.6% in the second quarter, according to data updated on 15 November 2026. The reading highlights a notable loss of support from the external sector after a positive contribution earlier in the year. The previous figure for the second quarter of 2026 showed external demand adding 0.6% compared with the first quarter, but the latest data indicate that exports minus imports are now dragging on overall GDP performance. On a quarter-over-quarter basis, the "actual" third-quarter change is measured against the second quarter, while the "previous" second-quarter increase is measured against the first quarter, underscoring the abrupt quarter-to-quarter turnaround. The negative print suggests that external factors—such as weaker overseas demand or stronger import growth—have shifted from being a tailwind to a headwind for Japan's economy in the third quarter, weakening one of the country's key growth pillars over the period. body: Japan's economic momentum reversed in the third quarter of 2026, with gross domestic product (GDP) contracting by 0.1% year-over-year, according to data updated on 15 November 2026. The reading marks a sharp turnaround from the second quarter of 2026, when GDP expanded by 1.7% compared with the same period a year earlier. The figures reflect a year-over-year comparison, meaning the current 0.1% decline in the third quarter is measured against the third quarter of the previous year, while the earlier 1.7% increase was measured against the second quarter a year prior. The shift from solid positive growth to a slight contraction underscores a weakening in Japan's economic trajectory as 2026 progresses. Analysts and investors will be watching upcoming data closely to assess whether this downturn proves temporary or signals a more persistent slowdown in Japan's recovery path. The latest numbers also raise questions over the policy mix needed to stabilize growth after the loss of momentum between the second and third quarters of 2026.
